analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare drug plans to pay pharmacies at least enough to cover the cost of buying and dispensing each drug.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee from June 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require Medicare drug plans to pay pharmacies at least enough to cover what each drug costs the pharmacy to buy and dispense, after subtracting any discounts or fees the plans take back. It would also create an appeal process for pharmacies paid below cost, require plans to disclose all the pricing pieces of each claim, and force plans to use standardized, independently developed performance measures instead of their own. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Community and independent pharmacies, especially in rural areas, would be guaranteed reimbursement that at least covers their cost to buy and dispense each Medicare-covered drug, plus a written appeal process when a plan pays below that floor. Patients benefit indirectly by keeping local pharmacies open and in-network. Pharmacy owners gain from restrictions on performance-based fees and new pricing transparency.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicare drug plans to pay network pharmacies, after all discounts and fees, at least what the pharmacy spent to acquire and dispense each covered drug, so small pharmacies are not dispensing at a loss.
Creates a written appeal process, through the Medicare Pharmaceutical and Technology Ombudsman, for pharmacies paid below their lowest actual acquisition and dispensing costs.

Requires plans to use standardized, independently developed pharmacy performance measures rather than their own targets, and to evaluate whether existing measures were achievable and applied uniformly across pharmacy types.
Requires plans to promptly disclose to pharmacies every pricing component of a claim, including fees, concessions, and incentives, ending opaque after-the-fact adjustments.

analysis.who_pays: Prescription drug plan sponsors, Medicare Advantage insurers, and the pharmacy benefit managers behind them, who would have to pay pharmacies enough to cover their actual costs and give up price concessions and performance-based fees not backed by standardized measures. Some of that cost could flow into Part D premiums and federal program spending.

drawbacks.text: Guaranteeing every pharmacy reimbursement that covers its full acquisition and dispensing costs would raise Medicare drug plan costs, some share of which would surface in premiums and federal spending rather than being absorbed by plans.
A federal payment floor limits plans' ability to negotiate lower drug dispensing prices, which is how many plans currently keep Part D drug spending down.

The bill targets pharmacy reimbursement but does not touch the rebate and formulary system through which PBMs extract concessions from manufacturers, so the larger PBM pricing structure would remain in place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is concrete: pharmacies across the country, especially independents and rural locations, have been closing as plan payments fall below what drugs cost them, and the bill would directly stop that by setting a cost-covering floor and an appeal process. The cost side is real but diffuse: higher guaranteed reimbursement would raise plan costs and some of it would show up in premiums and federal spending, and plans would lose some negotiating leverage. On balance the bill addressed a documented access problem for patients, and the fair criticism is less that it helps the wrong people than that it leaves the larger PBM rebate machinery untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 20, 2023 and referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Finance.
The action history shows no markup, hearing, committee vote, or floor action at any point in the two-year Congress; the last entry is the referral itself.
The bill drew a small bipartisan group of supporters, with cosponsors from both parties, but that support never translated into committee consideration.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died with it; identical language would have to be reintroduced in a new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicare drug plan sponsors, who continue to set pharmacy reimbursement and collect price concessions and performance fees without a federal cost floor, a pricing-claim disclosure requirement, or an appeal process for pharmacies. Large PBM-affiliated mail-order and specialty pharmacies keep their pricing advantages.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PBM-affiliated insurers keep paying pharmacies below cost

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: As Finance Committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration; the record shows no committee action after the June 20, 2023 referral

against.name: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicare drug plan industry
against.role: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicare drug plan sponsors
against.what_they_did: Have opposed federal requirements that Medicare plans pay pharmacies cost-covering reimbursement, which would reduce the concessions and fees they collect on pharmacy claims

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with one Democratic and two Republican cosponsors and drew no recorded opposition, but it never reached a vote in either chamber.

industries.note: The bill's core promise is a payment floor tied to each pharmacy's actual acquisition and dispensing costs, plus an appeal process when plans pay below that floor. Independent pharmacies, which lack the negotiating power of chains, would gain the most; rural patients gain through continued access.

The bill counts price concessions, discounts, fees, and incentives against pharmacies, so a plan could no longer pay a pharmacy less than the drug cost it. The bill also requires standardized performance measures and full claim pricing disclosure, cutting into PBM-driven fee and steerage revenue.

industries.industry: Medicare prescription drug plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: Plan sponsors would face a mandated minimum reimbursement and restrictions on performance-based fees and concessions, raising their Part D drug benefit costs.
The bill folds specialty pharmacies into the payment floor and requires the Secretary to define the term, limiting plans' ability to steer dispensing to their own lower-cost channels.
